steps.label: Conclusion (unlikely = opinion)
steps.body: It's unlikely that nanobes are living things.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: Nanobes are probably inanimate artifacts of the microscopic structure of the clay in which they're found.

steps.label: Evidence (because)
steps.body: Nanobes are 1/10 the size of the smallest known bacteria. They are too small to contain a reproductive mechanism, which is a prerequisite for life.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The whole argument rests on a rule and a fact. Rule: anything alive has a reproductive mechanism. Fact: a single nanobe is too small to contain one. Put them together and nanobes can't be alive, so the geologist must be looking at bits of clay.

Given that a single nanobe is too small to hold a reproductive mechanism, how could we still argue that nanobes are living things? We can't deny the rule; it's a premise. So look at what the author assumed about how the rule applies. The author assumes the mechanism has to fit inside one nanobe. What if nanobes don't reproduce one at a time? If several could team up, the group could have the mechanism that no single nanobe can hold.

A second route goes after the author's alternative: anything that makes "inanimate artifacts of the clay's microscopic structure" a poor explanation. That one is harder to predict, so expect the first route.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer showing that a living thing can reproduce without each individual containing the whole mechanism, for example by joining up with others. Less likely: an answer that makes the clay-artifact explanation hard to believe.

notes.body: A is about sexual reproduction in bacteria. The argument never said life requires sexual reproduction, only some reproductive mechanism, and bacteria reproduce in other ways. A says nothing about whether something one-tenth the size of a bacterium can reproduce, so the size problem is untouched.

The evidence only works if each nanobe has to carry its own reproductive mechanism. B breaks that assumption: "Single-celled creatures can combine to form a multicelled structure and then reproduce." Apply that to nanobes. One nanobe may be too small, but a group could reproduce together, so being tiny no longer rules out life.

The move to repeat: when you can't deny a premise, ask what the author assumed about how it applies, then find the answer that breaks the assumption. Here it was one individual, one mechanism.

C gives us material phenomena about the size of nanobes, but only says some scientists "claim" they are fossilized bacteria. Something nanobe-sized that we knew was alive would weaken badly. A disputed fossil isn't that, and it doesn't show anything that small ever had a reproductive mechanism.

D attacks old definitions of life built with "inferior microscopes no longer in use." The argument relies on one requirement, a reproductive mechanism, and D never says that requirement is wrong. The old definitions may have demanded the same thing. Nothing here helps a nanobe reproduce.

E says some animals are larger but simpler than others, so size and complexity don't line up perfectly. It runs the wrong way for us: we need something tiny that is still complex enough to reproduce, not something big and simple. And one fact about lizards says nothing about the scale of nanobes.

why: PT157/158 register: Evaluate and Goal were hedged and loose, and every note was padded or chatty (A argued itself in circles, B had a typo and no transferable move).

steps.label: Conclusion (thus)
steps.body: Children are put at the same risk for repetitive stress injuries as office workers.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion (Evidently)
steps.body: Most elementary school computers are installed without consideration of their effect on students' posture.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: In a study, all the keyboards and most monitors were placed higher than recommended for children, leading children to sit in ways that encourage craned necks, awkward wrists, and other unhealthy postures.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The argument makes two jumps, so there are two places to push.

Jump one: the computers are set too high, so they were installed "without consideration of their effect on posture." Given that all the keyboards and most monitors sit too high for children, how could someone still have considered posture? Maybe the computers are shared with adults and the height is a compromise. Possible, but a stretch.

Jump two is weaker. Given that children sit in unhealthy postures, how could they still not face "the same risk" as office workers? "Same" is a strong word. It assumes a child's body takes the same damage from bad posture that an adult's does, and that the exposure is comparable. Office workers sit at keyboards all day; children at school probably don't. And a child's body may handle strain differently. Either difference breaks "the same risk."

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that makes children different from office workers in a way that matters for repetitive stress injuries: less time at the computer, or bodies that handle the strain better. A less likely route: a good reason the computers were set high even though posture was considered.

notes.body: A says the recommended height differs for children and adults. The researcher already relied on that: the computers were "higher than recommended for children." A just explains why they count as too high, so it fits the evidence instead of challenging the jump to the same risk as office workers.

B is about time at home, but the conclusion is about the risk school computers create. More home use doesn't make the school postures any less harmful, and home setups could be just as bad. The impact is unclear, so B can't seriously weaken.

The researcher moves from bad posture straight to the same risk as office workers. That only works if a child's body reacts to strain the way an adult's does. C denies it: children's "greater suppleness" makes them "less susceptible than adults" to these injuries. Same postures, lower risk, so "the same risk" fails.

The move to repeat: when a conclusion says two groups are equal, look for a relevant difference between them.

D says office workers' equipment is usually at the wrong height too. That makes the two groups look more alike, which helps the comparison. To weaken, we need a difference between children and office workers, and D supplies a similarity.

E is about who reports injuries, not who gets them. Children might report fewer injuries simply because they don't recognize them or don't tell anyone. Reporting rates don't show their actual risk is lower, and the conclusion is about risk.

why: PT157/158 register: em-dash heavy, wrong-answer notes about 94 words of repetition, and the Evaluate step leaned on joke motives instead of the same-risk gap.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The health risks of GMO foods are minimal.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: A GMO food can't have effects that would be significant enough to be worrisome.

steps.label: Evidence (since)
steps.body: In most cases of deliberate alteration of a plant's genes, only a single gene in 750,000 has been changed. This change is very slight.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
There are two moves here, and we can push on either.

Move one, in the last sentence: the change is slight, so it "cannot have effects significant enough to be worrisome." Does that follow? Pull one block from the bottom of a Jenga tower and the whole thing comes down. What matters is not how much changed but what the changed part does. If a single gene controls something important, changing it could matter a lot.

Move two: "In most cases" only one gene in about 750,000 is changed, so the risk is minimal. Most cases aren't all cases. What if the foods people worry about are the ones where many genes were changed?

Move one is the bigger target. "Cannot" is a claim about every slight change, so a single counterexample hurts it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer showing that changing a single gene can have a significant, worrying effect. Less likely: an answer showing that engineered foods often involve more than a slight change, or direct evidence that their health risks are serious.

notes.body: A says engineered plants offer few advantages over ordinary ones. That's about benefits, and the scientist's conclusion is only about risk. A plant can be pointless and perfectly safe. A gives no reason to think a one-gene change can do harm.

B says whatever risks exist "may be somewhat reduced by other factors" such as added vitamins and minerals. That makes the risk smaller, if anything, which fits the claim that "the risk is minimal." A weakener needs the risk to be bigger than the scientist thinks.

C says scientists haven't located the genes behind every trait. That is uncertainty, and it cuts both ways: the changed gene might matter or might not. It never shows a one-gene change can have a significant effect. D gives a known case; C only gives a gap in knowledge.

The scientist's key move is that a change this slight "cannot have effects significant enough to be worrisome." D gives a counterexample: plants whose toxicity "is known to be affected by the alteration of a single gene." The toxicity in D is to animals, not people, but that is enough to break "cannot": one gene changed, and something as serious as toxicity changed with it. The size of a change doesn't decide its effect; what the gene does decides it.

The move to repeat: when an argument says something is too small to matter, look for a case where something that small mattered a lot.

E attacks the opponents: the consumers most opposed tend to be ill-informed. Even if the critics are wrong about everything, the scientist's own reasoning could still be bad. Undercutting the other side does nothing to the step from a slight change to no worrying effect.

why: PT157/158 register: em-dash heavy and padded, the B note misquoted the choice as risks reduced by cooking, and Evaluate/Goal had typos.

steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
steps.body: All animals can, in principle, be bred for domesticity.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Domesticated animals have come into existence by breeding only the tamest individuals of a wild species. If you breed only the individuals that show tameness when young, then after a number of generations you end up with a domesticated version of the animal, as with wolves becoming dogs.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion is huge: "all animals" can be bred for domesticity. The evidence is one method and one example, wolves. The method needs a starting point: individuals that show tameness when young.

So how could we argue that not all animals can be bred for domesticity?Find a species where the method can't start. Say we try it with hyenas, and no hyena pup in any litter ever shows tameness. There's nothing to select, so there's no way to keep breeding tame with tame.

Notice "in principle." The conclusion isn't saying domestication is easy or fast. A slow, difficult breeding program still counts. To weaken, we need the method to be impossible for some species, not just harder.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying some species have no members that ever display tameness, or anything else that makes the breeding method impossible, not merely slower, for at least one kind of animal.

notes.body: A is about the reverse trip: turning domesticated animals back into wild ones. The conclusion is only about breeding toward domesticity. Whether the trip back works says nothing about whether every species can make the trip forward.

B says wild members mate more often than tame ones in some species. That slows the program, but a breeder chooses which animals breed, so the tame ones can still be paired. The conclusion only claims domestication is possible "in principle," and B doesn't make it impossible.

The method only works if some individuals "display tameness when young." C removes that starting point for some species: "no members ever display tameness." No tame animals means nothing to select and nothing to breed, so those species can't be domesticated this way, and "all animals" fails.

The move to repeat: when a conclusion says all, one counterexample weakens it. Find what the method requires, then look for a case where the requirement is missing.

D is the tempting one, since tame members being "less fertile" sounds like a real obstacle. But less fertile still means fertile. The tame animals still have offspring, so the program just takes longer, and the conclusion only says domestication is possible "in principle." D would work only if tame members couldn't reproduce at all.

E is about species already domesticated: some members are tamer than others. That is variation after the process has succeeded. It tells us nothing about a wild species that has no tame members to start with.

why: Correct but padded PT157/158 notes with em dashes, plus typos in the Conclusion, Evidence, Evaluate and Goal steps; Evaluate never addressed "in principle", which is what kills B and D.

steps.label: Conclusion (So / clearly)
steps.body: Dr. Faris is in violation of the ethics code. Put another way: Dr. Faris deceived a patient about their medical treatment.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The ethics code says hospital staff must not deceive patients about their medical treatment. Dr. Faris gave medication A to a patient and said it would help the patient sleep, even though medication A has no known sleep-inducing properties. (The patient's sleep did improve after taking it.)

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion says Dr. Faris is "clearly" in violation. That depends on one thing: was the patient deceived? The only evidence of deception is that medication A has "no known sleep-inducing properties."

Given that, how could we argue Dr. Faris was honest in saying the medication would help the patient sleep? Look at the gap. A drug with no sleep-inducing properties can still help someone sleep by another route. Maybe it treats something that keeps the patient awake, like pain. The author even concedes that the patient's sleep did improve. If medication A helped through some indirect route, the statement was true, and a true statement isn't deception.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that gives medication A a real, indirect way to improve sleep, so that telling the patient it would help them sleep was true. That knocks out the deception, and the violation goes with it.

notes.body: A says Dr. Faris knew medication A had no known sleep-inducing properties. That makes the statement look more like knowing deception, not less. It strengthens the ethicist's case.
B says a committee is considering revisions to the code. The argument is about the code as it stands now. A possible future revision can't change whether Dr. Faris broke the current rule.

The ethicist treats "no known sleep-inducing properties" as if it meant the drug couldn't help anyone sleep. C pulls those apart: medication A "is a pain reliever that can indirectly lead to sleep" by easing discomfort. So telling the patient it would help them sleep was true, and a true statement isn't deception. No deception, no violation.

The move to repeat: when an argument calls a statement deceptive or false, look for a way the statement could be true after all.

D says other staff gave medication A to patients with trouble sleeping. Many people doing something doesn't make it honest. If the drug can't help with sleep, D only means more staff broke the code; it never gives a way the drug actually helps.

E rules out other medications as the reason the patient slept better. It's tempting, because it seems to point back to medication A. But sleep can improve for many reasons besides medication, and E gives no way medication A could help. C supplies that mechanism; E doesn't.

why: PT157/158 register (em dashes, 114-word wrong notes) plus gendered pronouns for Dr. Faris and the patient and a raw rephrase note in the Conclusion step.

steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
steps.body: The government should require drug companies to notify consumers of all known drug-related interactions.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Relatively minor drug-related interactions can still be harmful to patients (such as the fact that fruit juice can render aspirin ineffective, leading to people either not getting the pain relief they expected or to people taking more aspirin than necessary).

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
This is a recommendation, so ask what could go wrong with the plan. Given that relatively minor interactions can still hurt patients, as with aspirin and fruit juice, how could we argue the government should not require notice of "all known drug-related interactions"?

The author shows one upside. Look for downsides. Would it cost too much? Is it even possible? Could it backfire? Picture a drug insert listing forty interactions, most as mild as the fruit juice one. Would a patient still notice the one that could put them in the hospital? A plan meant to protect patients could end up hiding the warnings that matter most.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for a downside of requiring notice of every known interaction: it costs too much, it can't be done, or it backfires, for example by burying serious warnings under minor ones.

notes.body:
A shows the plan backfires. The advocate wants every interaction listed to protect patients. But listing minor ones "would detract from a patient’s attention to serious interactions." The plan meant to protect patients would leave them less protected from the interactions that matter most.

The move to repeat: on a recommendation, a strong weakener is a cost that undercuts the plan's own goal.

B says many drugs have fewer documented interactions than aspirin. That means shorter lists for those drugs, but the requirement still applies to them. Fewer interactions makes notice easier, if anything, so B gives no reason to drop the plan.

C says notice of every interaction would cause "only negligible price increases for consumers." Cost was a possible objection to the plan, and C takes it away. That helps the advocate. A weakener needs a real downside, not the removal of one.
D says many interactions haven't been identified yet. The plan only covers "all known" interactions, so the unknown ones are outside it. D shows no harm from listing the known ones.
E says pharmacists usually point patients to printed warnings. That suggests warnings actually get read, which makes notice look more useful. It strengthens the case for the plan.

why: PT157/158 register: em-dash heavy, padded notes, the C note distorted the choice into costs to drug companies, and the Goal step had an unclosed parenthesis.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The government's tax collection agency has not followed through on its plan to crack down on violations of corporate income tax law.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Audits are the primary tool for detecting corporate income tax violations, and over the past year since they announced the plan, not a single audit of corporate income tax returns has been completed.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The author's case: audits are the primary way to detect violations, no corporate audit has been completed in a year, so the agency hasn't followed through on its crackdown.

Given that not a single corporate audit was completed in the past year, how could we still argue the agency is following through? Look at the word "completed." The author assumes a real crackdown would produce finished audits within a year. What if audits take longer than that? Then the agency could have started hundreds of audits the day after the announcement, and the count of completed audits would still be zero.

Another route: the agency may be cracking down by other means. Audits are the "primary" tool, not the only one.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer that gives an innocent reason for zero completed audits, most likely that audits take more than a year to finish. Or an answer showing the agency is cracking down some other way.

notes.body: A says the crackdown is part of a broad campaign against corporate misconduct. That describes the plan's scope, not whether anything is being done. A broad campaign can still be doing nothing, and zero completed audits is just as unexplained.

B is about personal income tax audits; the crackdown is about corporate income tax law. More personal audits shows the agency is busy, but not with this plan. If anything, it makes the lack of corporate audits look like a choice.

C says most corporate audits don't turn up significant violations. That might make audits seem less worth doing, but it neither explains why none were completed nor shows any crackdown effort. The evidence of zero completed audits stands.

The argument assumes a real crackdown would show completed audits within a year. D says it "generally takes longer than one year to complete an audit." Now zero completed audits is exactly what we'd expect even if the agency began auditing the day it announced the plan. The evidence no longer points to inaction.

The move to repeat: when evidence counts results over a period, ask whether results could even arrive in that time.

E compares the last five years with the five before: fewer audits completed. That is a longer trend of doing less, which fits the idea that the agency isn't serious. It doesn't explain the past year's zero, so it can't weaken.

why: PT157/158 register: em dashes, notes averaging over 100 words with repetition, and an Evaluate step written in abbreviations (govt, corp).

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Whenever lawyers engage in obstructive behaviors (such as inflammatory language or badgering witnesses), it's reasonable to doubt whether the eventual verdict is correct.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: These obstructive behaviors hinder the jury's effort to reach a correct verdict.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The argument slides between two ideas.

Idea one: obstructive behavior hinders the jury's effort to reach a correct verdict.
Idea two: obstructive behavior makes it reasonable to doubt that a correct verdict was reached.

A strong headwind might hinder my effort to reach the top of Mt. Whitney. But if I'm standing at the summit, the headwind gives you no reason to doubt I got there.

Same here. Obstructive behavior can make the jury's job harder without making a wrong verdict likely. Given that these behaviors hinder the jury, how could we argue the verdict still deserves trust? Show that juries usually get past the obstruction anyway. And notice "Whenever": the conclusion covers every trial with such behavior, so anything showing the behavior rarely changes outcomes hurts it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying these behaviors rarely change what the jury decides, so even when lawyers use them, the verdict is probably still correct.

notes.body: A says strict judges sometimes preside over incorrect verdicts. The conclusion is about trials with obstructive behavior, and A is about trials without it. Wrong verdicts happening elsewhere doesn't show that badgering witnesses is harmless.

B says lawyers care less than judges about whether outcomes are just. That is about motives. The question is whether the tactics actually distort verdicts, and lawyers who care little about justice are, if anything, more likely to try.

C says people swayed by inflammatory language rarely admit it later. That makes the influence harder to detect, which gives us more reason to doubt verdicts, not less. It pushes toward the conclusion.

The conclusion needs obstructive behavior to actually threaten the verdict. D says it "is seldom effective in cases where jurors are also presented with legitimate evidence." In a typical trial jurors do hear legitimate evidence, so the badgering usually changes nothing, and the mere fact that it happened is weak grounds for doubting the verdict.

The move to repeat: when an argument goes from a hindrance to a doubtful result, look for an answer showing the job still gets done.
E says jurors are screened partly for bias. That happens before trial. A juror who starts out unbiased can still be swayed by badgering during it, so E doesn't show the behavior is harmless.

why: Correct analysis but PT157/158 register in the notes (em dashes, padding), and the Evaluate step put paraphrases in quotation marks.
